plain_english: So when you see a man wearing the purple robes of high office, and when you hear his name repeated constantly in the forum, don't envy him. He bought those things by throwing away years of his life. Men waste entire lifetimes just to have one year named after them as consul. Some die during the early struggle and never reach the heights they dreamed of. Others endure a thousand humiliations to reach that final honor, only to realize with misery that all their work will amount to nothing more than words carved on their tombstone.
original_excerpt: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life. Men throw away all their years in order to have one year named after them as consul: some lose their lives during the early part of the struggle, and never reach the height to which they aspired: some after having submitted to a thousand indignities in order to reach the crowning dignity, have the miserable reflexion that the only result of their labours will be the inscription on their tombstone.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 20

plain_english: Some people scold extreme old age for having the same foolish ambitions as youth. But then they collapse from weakness while chasing big, arrogant projects. What a shameful way to end — when your breath gives out in a courtroom while you're still trying to win over some ignorant crowd for some nobody client. How pathetic to die in the middle of your business dealings, worn out by life before you're worn out by work. And how embarrassing to drop dead while collecting money, with your heir laughing in the background after waiting so long for you to finally go.
original_excerpt: Some, while telling off extreme old age, like youth, for new aspirations, have found it fail from sheer weakness amid great and presumptuous enterprises. It is a shameful ending, when a man's breath deserts him in a court of justice, while, although well stricken in years, he is still striving to gain the sympathies of an ignorant audience for some obscure litigant: it is base to perish in the midst of one's business, wearied with living sooner than with working; shameful, too, to die in the act of receiving payments, amid the laughter of one's long-expectant heir.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 20

plain_english: I can't skip this story that comes to mind: Turannius was an extremely careful old man who had worked as a tax collector. When he turned ninety, Emperor Caius Caesar officially retired him from his job. So what did Turannius do? He had himself laid out on his bed like a corpse and mourned as if he were dead. His entire household mourned their old master's retirement. They didn't stop mourning until he got his job back. Can you believe it? Some people actually find joy in working themselves to death. Many others think the same way. They want to keep working long after their bodies can handle it. They fight against their physical weakness. They think old age is terrible for one reason only — because it forces them to stop working.
original_excerpt: I cannot pass over an an instance which occurs to me: Turannius was an old man of the most painstaking exactitude, who after entering upon his ninetieth year, when he had by G. Caesar's own act been relieved of his duties as collector of the revenue, ordered himself to be laid out on his bed and mourned for as though he were dead. The whole house mourned for the leisure of its old master, and did not lay aside its mourning until his work was restored to him. Can men find such pleasure in dying in harness? Yet many are of the same mind: they retain their wish for labour longer than their capacity for it, and fight against their bodily weakness; they think old age an evil for no other reason than because it lays them on the shelf.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 20

plain_english: The law won't make a soldier serve past fifty or require a senator to show up past sixty. But people have a harder time giving themselves permission to rest than getting legal permission. Meanwhile, they keep stealing from each other and getting robbed in return. They disturb each other's peace and make everyone miserable. Life becomes pointless — no profit, no pleasure, no growth. No one remembers they're going to die. No one stops making grand plans for the distant future. Some even plan things that will happen after they're dead: massive tombs, public monuments, elaborate funeral games, and showy processions. But honestly, these people's funerals should be held with just a few torches and candles — as if they had only lived a few days.
original_excerpt: The law does not enrol a soldier after his fiftieth year, or require a senator's attendance after his sixtieth: but men have more difficulty in obtaining their own consent than that of the law to a life of leisure. Meanwhile, while they are plundering and being plundered, while one is disturbing another's repose, and all are being made wretched alike, life remains without profit, without pleasure, without any intellectual progress: no one keeps death well before his eyes, no one refrains from far-reaching hopes. Some even arrange things which lie beyond their own lives, such as huge sepulchral buildings, the dedication of public works, and exhibitions to be given at their funeral-pyre, and ostentatious processions: but, by Hercules, the funerals of such men ought to be conducted by the light of torches and wax tapers, as though they had lived but a few days.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 20
